items.title: Eyewitness memories can be planted
items.claim: Elizabeth Loftus's lab implanted entirely false childhood memories in adult participants. What proportion came to believe the fake event was real?
items.reveal_title: About a quarter of people 'remembered' something that never happened
items.reveal:
In the 'Lost in the Mall' study (Loftus & Pickrell, 1995), 25% of participants came to recall a fabricated childhood event after being told by a family member it had occurred.

Later work with more vivid scenarios reached implantation rates around 50%.
items.why: Memory feels like recording. It is reconstruction, and reconstruction is suggestible.

items.title: Milgram's obedience rate
items.claim: In Stanley Milgram's 1963 baseline experiment, participants were ordered to deliver what they believed were increasing electric shocks to a stranger. What proportion went all the way to the maximum 450 volts?
items.reveal_title: Around 65% continued to the maximum level
items.reveal:
In Milgram's original Yale study (1963), 26 of 40 participants (65%) continued to the 450V switch under verbal pressure from the experimenter.

Replications, including Burger (2009) in modified form, found broadly similar obedience patterns.
items.why: Situational pressure from a perceived authority figure can override personal moral judgement to a degree most people predict incorrectly.

items.title: The magical number seven
items.claim: George Miller's 1956 paper proposed a famous limit on short-term memory. What was the span?
items.reveal:
Miller's 1956 paper 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two' described short-term memory span as roughly 5 to 9 items.

Later work by Cowan (2001) revised the effective limit to around 4 chunks once rehearsal is controlled.
items.why: Capacity depends on how information is grouped. Chunking effectively expands what fits in working memory.

items.title: Asch's conformity finding
items.claim: In Solomon Asch's 1950s line-judgement studies, participants gave an obviously wrong answer to match the group. Across all critical trials, what proportion of responses conformed to the incorrect majority?
items.reveal:
Asch (1955) found roughly 37% of responses on critical trials matched the incorrect majority. About 75% of participants conformed on at least one trial.

With just one dissenting confederate, conformity dropped sharply.
items.why: Conformity is real and measurable but partial. Most answers across all trials remained correct.

items.title: The bystander effect story
items.claim: Darley and Latane (1968) showed that people are less likely to help when others are present. The often-repeated 'Kitty Genovese 38 witnesses' story has been challenged. What did later journalism find?
items.prompt: Which is closest to the current historical record?

options.text: There were probably far fewer witnesses than reported, and some did call police
There were no witnesses at all

items.reveal:
Manning, Levine and Collins (2007) and later reporting by the New York Times showed the original 1964 article overstated the number of witnesses and inattention.

The bystander effect as a laboratory phenomenon is robust, but the case used to illustrate it was inaccurate.
items.why: Findings can be real while their iconic illustrations are not. Textbooks now distinguish the experimental effect from the journalistic story.

items.title: What Pavlov was actually studying
items.claim: Ivan Pavlov is famous for ringing bells at dogs. What was he originally researching when he noticed conditioned responses?
items.reveal_title: He won a Nobel Prize for digestion, not psychology
items.reveal:
Pavlov received the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on the digestive system.

The conditioned salivation finding emerged as a by-product of measuring gastric secretion in dogs.
items.why: Many landmark psychological findings began as observations inside other disciplines.

items.title: Phineas Gage's recovery
items.claim: In 1848 an iron rod passed through the frontal lobe of railroad worker Phineas Gage. He survived. How long did he live afterwards?
items.reveal_title: Gage lived for roughly 12 more years
items.reveal:
Gage died in 1860 after epileptic seizures. Recent scholarship (Macmillan, 2000) suggests his personality changes were less extreme and more temporary than the textbook caricature implies.

He worked as a stagecoach driver in Chile in his later years.
items.why: Famous case studies are often simplified in retelling. Lesion evidence is more nuanced than the headline.

items.title: What split-brain patients reveal
items.claim: Roger Sperry's split-brain research (Nobel Prize 1981) studied patients whose corpus callosum had been severed to treat what condition?
items.reveal_title: The surgery was a last-resort epilepsy treatment
items.reveal:
Commissurotomy was performed to prevent seizures from spreading between hemispheres. Sperry and Gazzaniga then used these patients to study hemispheric specialisation in the 1960s and 70s.

The research showed each hemisphere could process information independently when communication was cut.
items.why: Some of the most important findings about the brain came from rare clinical populations.

items.title: Attachment classifications
items.claim: Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation (1970s) identified attachment styles in infants. In the original US sample, what proportion were classified as securely attached?
items.reveal_title: Roughly two thirds were classified secure
items.reveal:
Ainsworth (1978) reported about 66% secure, 22% insecure-avoidant, 12% insecure-resistant.

Main and Solomon (1990) later added a fourth category, disorganised attachment.
items.why: Distributions vary by culture. Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's 1988 meta-analysis showed cross-cultural variation in the proportions.

items.title: What we know about Little Albert
items.claim: John Watson and Rosalie Rayner's 1920 'Little Albert' study conditioned an infant to fear a white rat. What is now believed about the child's identity?

options.text: His identity was always public knowledge
Later researchers proposed identifications but no consensus exists
He grew up to become a famous psychologist
Records confirm he kept the conditioned fear for life

items.reveal:
Beck, Levinson and Irons (2009) proposed Douglas Merritte; Powell et al. (2014) proposed William Barger. The case remains unresolved.

The study itself would not meet modern ethical standards for research with infants.
items.why: Ethical reviews now prevent such studies. Their existence in the historical record shapes how we teach research ethics today.

items.title: The serotonin hypothesis
items.claim: A 2022 umbrella review by Moncrieff et al. examined the link between serotonin and depression. What did it conclude?

options.text: Strong evidence supports the simple chemical-imbalance model
It found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin
It confirmed dopamine is the primary cause
It showed antidepressants do not work at all

items.reveal_title: The simple chemical-imbalance story is not well supported
items.reveal:
Moncrieff et al. (2022, Molecular Psychiatry) found no convincing evidence that depression is caused by reduced serotonin activity.

The review did not address whether antidepressants help, only whether the serotonin-deficit model holds.
items.why: Effective treatments do not require correct causal stories. Aspirin was used long before its mechanism was understood.

items.title: What Dunning and Kruger actually showed
items.claim: Dunning and Kruger (1999) reported a finding that became internet shorthand. Their actual graph showed something subtler. Which is closest?

options.text: The least competent rated themselves below average
Most people overestimated their performance; the lowest performers overestimated the most
The most competent thought they were the worst

items.reveal_title: Most people overestimated; the least competent overestimated most
items.reveal:
In the original study, participants in the bottom quartile of test performance rated themselves around the 62nd percentile.

Statisticians (Nuhfer et al., 2017) have argued part of the effect is regression to the mean rather than pure metacognitive failure.
items.why: Popular versions of findings often lose the nuance that makes them scientifically interesting.

items.title: Re-evaluating Stanford Prison
items.claim: Philip Zimbardo's 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment is often cited as proof that situations dictate behaviour. What did later archival work by Le Texier and others reveal?

options.text: Guards received explicit coaching, undermining the 'natural' interpretation
No participant played the guard role

items.reveal_title: Guards were coached, not spontaneously behaving
items.reveal:
Le Texier's 2018 archival analysis and a 2019 American Psychologist article showed guards received briefings encouraging tough behaviour.

The BBC Prison Study (Reicher & Haslam, 2006) produced very different dynamics under similar setup.
items.why: Replication and archival work reshape how landmark findings are interpreted.

items.title: Growth mindset meta-analyses
items.claim: Carol Dweck's growth mindset theory inspired large-scale school interventions. What did Sisk et al.'s 2018 meta-analysis report about the effect on academic achievement?

options.text: Very large positive effects in all settings
Small effects on average, larger for at-risk students

items.reveal:
Sisk et al. (2018) found a weak overall correlation between mindset and achievement, with stronger effects among lower-attaining and at-risk groups.

A 2019 US national experiment (Yeager et al.) found small but real gains for lower-achieving high schoolers.
items.why: Educational interventions rarely produce uniform effects across populations.

items.title: Bowlby's 44 thieves
items.claim: John Bowlby's 1944 '44 Juvenile Thieves' study linked maternal separation to later antisocial behaviour. What is a key methodological criticism made of it today?

options.text: The sample was very large and well controlled
Bowlby personally interviewed the children, risking confirmation bias, and the sample was small
It was a randomised controlled trial

items.reveal:
Bowlby studied 44 juvenile thieves and 44 controls at his clinic, conducting assessments himself. Critics note the risk of bias and the difficulty of separating maternal deprivation from broader disadvantage.

Rutter (1981) drew the influential distinction between privation and deprivation.
items.why: Foundational studies often used methods we would now strengthen, but they framed questions that still drive research.

items.title: The multi-store model was too simple for working memory
items.claim: Atkinson and Shiffrin's 1968 multi-store model split memory into sensory, short-term and long-term stores. What replaced its account of short-term memory?

options.text: Nothing — the multi-store model is unchanged

Baddeley and Hitch's 1974 working memory model — a central executive coordinating a phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and (later) episodic buffer — better fitted evidence that STM is not a single unitary store

items.reveal:
Patients with impaired STM (e.g., KF, studied by Shallice and Warrington 1970) could nonetheless retain visual information and form new long-term memories — evidence STM had components. Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed a multi-component working memory. The episodic buffer was added by Baddeley in 2000.

The multi-store model is still taught as a stepping stone but is superseded for STM specifically.
items.why: Models that fit the original data often fail later, more specific data. Working memory's multiple components matter for education, clinical assessment and cognitive neuroscience.

items.title: Long-term memory is not one system
items.claim: Endel Tulving distinguished episodic and semantic memory. What is the key difference?

options.text: Episodic stores facts; semantic stores experiences

Episodic memory is autobiographical and time-stamped (your breakfast this morning); semantic is general knowledge (London is the UK capital). Procedural memory (how to ride a bike) is a third, separate system

items.reveal:
Patient HM (Henry Molaison) could not form new episodic memories after his 1953 surgery but retained semantic knowledge from before the operation and could acquire new procedural skills (motor mirror-tracing).

Neuroimaging (Tulving, Nyberg, Cabeza 2000s) supports differential activation: hippocampus crucial for episodic; widespread cortical networks for semantic; basal ganglia/cerebellum for procedural. Different forms of dementia (semantic dementia vs Alzheimer's) damage these systems differently.
items.why: Treating memory as a single capacity misses clinically and educationally important distinctions. Memory loss patterns reveal architecture.

items.title: Bartlett showed memory reconstructs around schemas
items.claim: Frederic Bartlett's 1932 'War of the Ghosts' study asked British participants to recall a Native American folk tale. What pattern emerged?

options.text: Participants progressively rationalised the story to fit British cultural schemas — omitting culturally unfamiliar elements, shortening, replacing 'canoes' with 'boats' — demonstrating reconstructive memory

items.reveal:
Bartlett's 'Remembering' (1932) introduced 'schemas' to cognitive psychology. Participants' recall after weeks or months showed systematic distortions consistent with making the story 'make sense' in their own cultural framework.

Methodological critics note Bartlett's loose instructions and lack of statistical analysis. The schema concept has been operationalised more rigorously since (Brewer & Treyens 1981 office study; Loftus on eyewitness memory).
items.why: Memory is not playback. The same mechanism that lets us remember efficiently makes us systematically misremember in predictable ways.

items.title: Cognitive load theory shapes instructional design
items.claim: John Sweller's cognitive load theory (1988 onwards) distinguishes three types of load. Which design principle follows directly?

options.text: Always make instructions as long as possible

Minimise extraneous load (poor design) and manage intrinsic load (task complexity) so working memory can devote capacity to germane load (schema formation) — worked examples for novices, problem-solving for experts (expertise reversal effect)

items.reveal_title: Working memory is the bottleneck for learning
items.reveal:
Sweller's theory builds on Miller's 7+/-2 and Baddeley's working memory. Educational applications include worked-example effect (better than problem-solving for novices), modality effect (combining visual + auditory exceeds visual alone), redundancy effect (repeating information harms learning).

David Geary distinguishes 'biologically primary' knowledge (language, faces) that we acquire effortlessly from 'biologically secondary' (reading, algebra) that requires designed instruction. The theory has reshaped UK curriculum guidance (EEF 2018, Ofsted 2019).
items.why: Teaching that ignores working memory limits — long instructions, complex diagrams, novice problem-solving — is measurably less effective. CLT puts a constraint into instructional design.

items.title: Sperry's Nobel work showed hemispheres process independently
items.claim: Roger Sperry's split-brain research (Nobel 1981) found that when the corpus callosum is severed and images shown to only one visual field, what happens?

options.text: Both hemispheres still share all information
An object shown only to the left visual field (right hemisphere) cannot be named verbally (because language is typically left-hemisphere lateralised) but can be selected by touch with the left hand

items.reveal_title: Hemispheres can act independently after callosotomy
items.reveal:
Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga studied epilepsy patients who had undergone callosotomy. Their experiments showed each hemisphere could process information without conscious awareness in the other, raising deep questions about the unity of consciousness.

The popular 'left-brain logical, right-brain creative' caricature is wildly oversimplified — both hemispheres contribute to most cognitive tasks in intact brains. Lateralisation is real but localised to specific functions (language, visuospatial processing).
items.why: Findings about rare clinical populations can constrain theories of normal cognition. The popular interpretation often outruns the evidence.

items.title: Gage's personality change was real but exaggerated in retelling
items.claim: The story of Phineas Gage (1848) is widely taught as a sudden, permanent personality transformation. What does modern scholarship suggest?

options.text: He was permanently and severely changed forever

Personality changes occurred but Macmillan (2000) and others find evidence of substantial recovery over time; Gage worked as a stagecoach driver in Chile for years, requiring social and planning skills
Gage was unaffected by the injury

items.reveal:
Malcolm Macmillan's 'An Odd Kind of Fame' (2000) compiled the historical record. After his 1848 accident, Gage worked at a livery stable in New Hampshire, then drove a long-distance stagecoach in Valparaiso, Chile (1852-59) — a demanding job requiring planning, social interaction and route management.

He died in 1860 after a series of seizures. The neuroimaging reconstructions of his injury (Damasio et al. 1994, Van Horn et al. 2012) suggest damage to left frontal regions and white matter tracts.

The textbook story ('No longer Gage') exaggerates permanence.
items.why: Iconic case studies become simplified in retelling. The brain's capacity for functional reorganisation matters for both clinical practice and theory.

items.title: HM could form new procedural but not episodic memories
items.claim: Henry Molaison (HM) had bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in 1953 for severe epilepsy. After the operation:

options.text: He had no memory of any kind
He could not form new conscious (declarative) memories but could acquire procedural skills like mirror-tracing — improving with practice while denying ever having done the task
He recovered fully within a year
He became a famous psychologist himself

items.reveal:
Brenda Milner began studying HM in 1955. Her 1962 paper documented procedural learning despite dense anterograde amnesia. HM died in 2008; his identity was revealed posthumously. His brain was sliced into 2,401 sections (Annese et al. 2014) and photographed, available online.

His case established that medial temporal lobe (especially hippocampus) is essential for new declarative memory formation but not for procedural learning. Suzanne Corkin worked with HM for 46 years.
items.why: Single-case neuropsychology can produce findings that constrain theories of normal cognition for generations. The dissociation between memory systems was visible in one patient.

items.title: Shift work has measurable long-term health effects
items.claim: The WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer classified shift work involving circadian disruption as 'probably carcinogenic to humans' (Group 2A) in 2007. What was the basis?

options.text: Meta-analyses of cohort studies linking long-term night shift work with breast cancer risk; mechanisms include melatonin suppression by light at night and metabolic disruption

items.reveal:
IARC reaffirmed the Group 2A classification in 2019. The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young for discovering molecular mechanisms of circadian rhythms (PER, TIM, CLOCK genes).

Shift-work-associated risks documented: increased rates of metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, depression and certain cancers. Effects are dose-dependent on years of shift work. Denmark's National Board of Industrial Injuries pays compensation for breast cancer following long-term night shift work.
items.why: Biological rhythms aren't a lifestyle preference; sustained disruption has measurable health consequences. Workplace design implications follow.

items.title: Bowlby's monotropy claim has been substantially revised
items.claim: John Bowlby's original theory emphasised a single primary attachment figure (typically the mother). What does subsequent evidence suggest?

options.text: Monotropy is fully supported by all evidence

Infants form attachment hierarchies with multiple caregivers (Schaffer & Emerson 1964); fathers, grandparents and consistent non-parental carers can serve as attachment figures; quality matters more than exclusivity
Only mothers can be attachment figures

items.reveal:
Schaffer and Emerson's 1964 Glasgow study followed 60 babies and found by 18 months most had multiple attachments; nearly a third had primary attachment to someone other than the mother. Lamb's (2010) reviews of father involvement showed independent contributions to child outcomes.

The monotropy claim, alongside Bowlby's earlier ideas about 'maternal deprivation', shaped 1950s-60s policy (working mothers, daycare, hospital visiting). Rutter's 'Maternal Deprivation Reassessed' (1972) sharpened the distinction between privation (no attachment formed) and deprivation (loss of formed attachment).
items.why: Theories with policy implications need re-examination as evidence accumulates. Bowlby's core insight (attachment relationships matter) survives; the specific claim of monotropy has been substantially revised.

items.title: The Strange Situation has cultural biases
items.claim: Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's 1988 meta-analysis of Strange Situation studies across 8 countries found what pattern?

options.text: Identical proportions of attachment types in all cultures

Higher rates of insecure-avoidant in Germany and insecure-resistant in Japan and Israel — but interpretation is contested: are these real attachment differences or measurement artefacts of an American-developed procedure?
The Strange Situation cannot be administered outside the US
No cultural variation exists in any developmental measure

items.reveal:
Takahashi (1990) noted Japanese infants are rarely left alone, so the Strange Situation may induce extreme distress that registers as 'resistant'. German samples (Grossmann) showed avoidance interpreted differently — culturally valued early independence.

IJzendoorn's later work (1999, 2008) emphasised within-culture variation often exceeds between-culture. The procedure's validity outside Western middle-class contexts remains debated.
items.why: Standardised procedures developed in one culture may measure different things in another. Cross-cultural psychology often needs methodological adaptation, not just translation.

items.title: Piaget underestimated young children's abilities
items.claim: Piaget's three-mountains task (1956) found children under 7 are 'egocentric' — unable to take another's perspective. What did later work show?

options.text: Piaget's stages are timed exactly correctly

When the task is made more naturalistic (Hughes's policeman doll task, 1975), 3-4 year olds succeed; Piaget's task underestimated perspective-taking ability. False-belief tasks (Wimmer & Perner 1983) reveal more nuanced developmental trajectories

items.reveal:
Martin Hughes's 1975 'naughty boy hiding from policeman' task gave familiar context: ~90% of 3-4 year olds succeeded. Theory of mind (false belief) emerges around age 4; precursors are present earlier in non-verbal tasks (Onishi & Baillargeon 2005).

Piaget's broader staircase model — distinct, age-defined stages with sharp transitions — has been replaced by more gradualist accounts in modern developmental cognitive neuroscience.
items.why: Famous developmental milestones can shift dramatically with task design. Children often know more than the original tasks could reveal.

items.title: Vygotsky's ZPD emphasised social learning
items.claim: Lev Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (work in 1920s-30s, popularised in West from 1962 onwards) describes:

options.text: The gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help from a more knowledgeable other — emphasising social context as constitutive of cognitive development
A physical region of the brain
A stage of motor development only

items.reveal:
Vygotsky died in 1934 aged 37. His work was suppressed in Stalin's USSR and reached the West in translation (Thought and Language, 1962; Mind in Society, 1978).

'Scaffolding' was Bruner's term (Wood, Bruner & Ross 1976) capturing the temporary support that enables a learner to reach beyond independent ability. Modern educational applications: peer tutoring, guided discovery, gradual release of responsibility models.
items.why: Vygotsky's emphasis on social context contrasts with Piaget's relatively solitary child. Modern developmental psychology integrates both — children develop through cultural participation, not despite it.

items.title: Placebo effects are real but smaller than often claimed
items.claim: Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche's 2010 Cochrane meta-analysis of 234 trials of placebo versus no treatment found:

options.text: Placebos rivalled active drugs for most conditions
Placebos had small effects on continuous subjective outcomes (especially pain and nausea); little effect on objective outcomes; placebo effect in everyday discourse exaggerates the clinical evidence
Placebos had no measurable effect at all

items.reveal:
Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche's Cochrane review pooled randomised trials comparing placebo with no treatment. Effects on objective outcomes (blood pressure, tumour size) were near zero; effects on subjective ones (pain ratings, anxiety) were measurable but modest.

Open-label placebos (Kaptchuk et al. 2010) — patients told they're receiving placebo — still produce effects for some conditions, suggesting expectation and clinical ritual play roles beyond deception.
items.why: Placebos matter for clinical trial design (controls), patient communication and understanding what 'treatment effect' means — but the popular framing oversells what placebos can do.

items.title: Chronic stress activates the HPA axis
items.claim: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis produces cortisol in response to stress. What does chronic activation cause?

options.text: Sustained elevation of cortisol is associated with immune suppression, abdominal fat deposition, hippocampal atrophy, and increased cardiovascular risk — moving stress from a psychological to a physiological problem
Cortisol stops being produced under chronic stress

items.reveal:
Hans Selye described the General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm, resistance, exhaustion) in 1936. Bruce McEwen's concept of 'allostatic load' (1998) extends this: the wear-and-tear of repeated stress responses contributes to chronic disease.

Whitehall studies (Marmot, 1967 onwards) linked low job control with worse health outcomes via stress pathways. The relationship between psychosocial stress and cardiovascular disease is robust across cohorts but causality is hard to isolate from confounders.
items.why: The mind-body distinction breaks down when looking at chronic stress. Psychological experience produces measurable biological change with health consequences.

items.title: Type A personality's link to heart disease has weakened
items.claim: Friedman and Rosenman's 1959 'Type A' personality (competitive, impatient, hostile) was linked to coronary heart disease. What does the more recent evidence show?

options.text: Type A is the strongest predictor of heart disease
The composite Type A construct has weak predictive value in modern studies; hostility specifically (Williams 1989 onwards) retains some predictive power, while time-urgency and competitiveness do not
Type A reduces heart disease risk

items.reveal_title: Hostility, not the full Type A
items.reveal:
Friedman and Rosenman's 1976 follow-up of the Western Collaborative Group Study showed Type A nearly doubled CHD risk. Meta-analyses since the 1990s (Myrtek 2001) found weak overall effects for Type A; hostility/anger components retained predictive power.

The broader pattern: complex personality categories often decompose under empirical scrutiny into more specific traits with different effects.
items.why: Popular psychology preserves the original construct long after research has narrowed it. Specific hostility, not generic 'Type A', is what carries the cardiovascular signal.

items.title: Locus of control predicts health behaviours
items.claim: Julian Rotter's 1966 locus of control distinguishes internal (own actions cause outcomes) and external (luck, others, fate). How does it relate to health?

options.text: Locus of control has no link to health
Internal locus correlates modestly with adherence to medical regimens, exercise and other health behaviours; but it can also lead to self-blame when illness occurs despite effort

items.reveal:
Wallston's Multidimensional Health Locus of Control scale (1978) refined Rotter's construct for health applications. Meta-analyses (Norman et al. 1998) find modest correlations between internal HLOC and health behaviours.

Caveats: structural factors (income, access to care, environment) often dwarf locus of control's effect. Heavy 'personal responsibility' framing can ignore upstream determinants of health.
items.why: Individual-level psychological variables matter for health behaviours but operate within structural constraints. Both levels of analysis are needed.

items.title: The Health Belief Model predicts (some) preventive behaviours
items.claim: Rosenstock's 1974 Health Belief Model proposes that preventive behaviour depends on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers. What's its empirical track record?

options.text: It predicts all health behaviours perfectly

Meta-analyses (Carpenter 2010) find modest predictive power: perceived barriers strongest, perceived benefits moderate, susceptibility and severity weaker. The model under-weights social and emotional factors
It only applies to dental hygiene

items.reveal:
Rosenstock developed the HBM from 1950s public health work on TB screening uptake. It has been applied to vaccination, screening, smoking cessation and COVID behaviours.

Competitors and extensions: Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen 1991, adds intention and perceived control); Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska 1979, stages of change). Behavioural economics (EAST framework: easy, attractive, social, timely) is the more recent UK policy framework.
items.why: Behaviour-change theories provide testable frameworks but rarely explain more than a fraction of variance. Combining them with structural interventions usually outperforms either alone.

items.title: Smoking cessation works best with combined intervention
items.claim: Cochrane reviews of smoking cessation find that brief GP advice has what effect compared with no intervention?

options.text: Brief advice produces a small absolute increase (~2-3 percentage points) in quit rates; combined with NRT or varenicline plus behavioural support, quit rates can reach 25%+ at 6 months
Brief advice has the strongest effect of any intervention

items.reveal_title: Small effects scale to population health gains
items.reveal:
Stead et al.'s Cochrane reviews of brief physician advice find risk ratio ~1.66 for quitting compared with usual care. Translated to absolute risk: ~2-3 percentage points. Per intervention this seems small; applied across millions of patient encounters it represents very large population health gains.

NRT (Hartmann-Boyce et al.) approximately doubles quit rates; varenicline more so; combined pharmacotherapy plus intensive behavioural support is most effective.
items.why: Effective health interventions don't always have large per-person effects; they can have large per-population effects. Public health works on different scales than individual clinical practice.

items.title: Inverted-U is more nuanced than the textbook curve
items.claim: The Yerkes-Dodson law (1908) proposes an inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance. What is the modern refinement?

options.text: Optimal arousal varies with task complexity (simple tasks tolerate higher arousal) and skill level. Hanin's Individual Zones of Optimal Functioning (IZOF, 1980s) shows the optimal level varies between individuals
Arousal has no effect on performance

items.reveal_title: Inverted-U, but where the peak sits varies
items.reveal:
Yerkes and Dodson's original 1908 study used mice learning brightness discrimination. The 'law' has been extended far beyond its evidence base.

Yuri Hanin's IZOF model treats optimal arousal as individual: some elite athletes perform best when relaxed, others when highly aroused. The catastrophe theory (Hardy & Fazey, 1987) adds that under high cognitive anxiety, performance can collapse sharply rather than smoothly.
items.why: A single curve hides large individual differences. Coaches who treat arousal management as one-size-fits-all miss what makes elite athletes different.

items.title: Flow requires challenge matching skill
items.claim: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's flow research (1975 onwards) identified conditions for the optimal experience. What characterises flow?

options.text: Challenge matched to skill (slightly stretching), clear goals, immediate feedback, deep concentration, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, time distortion

items.reveal:
Csikszentmihalyi's Experience Sampling Method (ESM, 1975) gave participants pagers; when paged at random they noted what they were doing and how they felt. The pattern: deep enjoyment occurred when skill and challenge were both high.

Too little challenge → boredom; too much → anxiety. Sports psychology uses flow frameworks for performance preparation. Critics (Engeser 2012) note flow may be more available in certain activity types and that measurement post-hoc is suspect.
items.why: Flow describes a measurable state but doesn't make it easy to engineer. The conditions can be designed for; the experience can't be commanded.

items.title: Choking is more than just nerves
items.claim: Sian Beilock and colleagues' research on choking under pressure identifies two mechanisms. Which?

options.text: Distraction (anxiety occupies working memory needed for the task) and explicit monitoring (conscious attention to automatic motor skills disrupts them) — different mechanisms suggest different interventions

items.reveal:
Beilock and Carr (2001, 2005) showed expert golfers putted worse when paying conscious attention to their swing; novices benefited from explicit instruction.

Distraction-based choking responds to attention training and pre-performance routines; monitoring-based choking responds to maintaining flow-state distraction (focusing on external targets rather than mechanics). The dual-process model has reshaped elite athlete preparation.
items.why: Choking has identifiable mechanisms with specific countermeasures. Generic 'stay calm' advice misses both.

items.title: DSM categories don't always carve nature at the joints
items.claim: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual is the standard US classification of mental disorders. What's the standard critique?

options.text: DSM categories perfectly match underlying biology

Categories were chosen by committee consensus; high comorbidity between disorders, dimensional features within categories, and biological heterogeneity all suggest DSM may not reflect natural kinds. The NIH RDoC (Research Domain Criteria, 2010) proposes a dimensional alternative for research
DSM has only one category for all disorders

items.reveal:
DSM-5 (2013) maintained categorical diagnosis under pressure to introduce dimensional aspects. Thomas Insel (then NIMH director) announced in 2013 that NIMH would 're-orient' research away from DSM categories toward RDoC.

Key problems: ~60% of patients meet criteria for two or more disorders simultaneously; treatment response often crosses diagnostic boundaries; genetic studies (Cross-Disorder Group, 2013) show overlapping risk variants across disorders.

ICD-11 (WHO, 2022) introduced some dimensional elements.
items.why: Diagnostic categories shape research, insurance and stigma. The categories matter clinically even where their scientific basis is questioned.

items.title: CBT works for depression — with caveats
items.claim: Cuijpers and colleagues' meta-analyses of CBT for depression report effect sizes in the moderate range. What's the most important methodological caveat?

options.text: Most trials have substantial risk of bias (publication bias, lack of blinding, allegiance effects when researchers favour the treatment); effect sizes may be inflated by 20-50%
CBT only works for healthy people

items.reveal:
Pim Cuijpers's group has published numerous meta-analyses (Cuijpers et al. 2010, 2014, 2019). They consistently find CBT and other structured psychotherapies effective for depression but with methodological caveats: many trials are not blinded (impossible for psychotherapy), researcher allegiance correlates with effect size, publication bias remains an issue.

The NHS's IAPT (Improving Access to Psychological Therapies, 2008) made CBT widely available; routine outcomes data show recovery rates around 50% within treatment, lower than RCTs.
items.why: Treatment efficacy is layered: works in trials, sometimes less well in routine practice. The research-practice gap matters for service planning.

items.title: Antidepressant effects have been distorted by publication bias
items.claim: Turner et al.'s 2008 NEJM analysis compared published antidepressant trials with those registered with the FDA. What did they find?

options.text: Of 74 registered trials, 38 positive trials were nearly all published (37/38) while 36 negative or questionable trials were largely unpublished or recast as positive — inflating apparent efficacy by ~32%

items.reveal_title: What's published is not what's done
items.reveal:
Turner, Matthews, Linardatos, Tell & Rosenthal (NEJM 2008) used FDA records covering 12 antidepressants. Cipriani et al. (Lancet 2018) meta-analysed all available antidepressant trials and found small but real effect sizes, with substantial variation between drugs.

Resulting reforms: ClinicalTrials.gov pre-registration (2007 US law); EU mandatory reporting; the AllTrials campaign. Bias has reduced but not disappeared.
items.why: Evidence-based medicine depends on the available evidence being representative. Publication bias systematically distorts apparent treatment effects.

items.title: The lobotomy was awarded a Nobel Prize
items.claim: Egas Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discovery of the therapeutic value of the prefrontal leucotomy (lobotomy). What's the modern status?

options.text: The procedure remains a first-line treatment

Lobotomy is no longer performed; thousands of patients (around 40,000-50,000 in the US alone, 1936-50s) suffered permanent personality damage. Modern psychosurgery is far more targeted (deep brain stimulation, cingulotomy for refractory OCD)

items.reveal_title: An honoured procedure that caused immense harm
items.reveal:
Walter Freeman performed perhaps 3,500 of his transorbital 'icepick' lobotomies in the US through the 1950s. Patients included Rosemary Kennedy (1941, permanently incapacitated) and many institutionalised individuals.

The procedure declined rapidly after chlorpromazine (1952) provided pharmacological alternatives. Calls to revoke Moniz's Nobel continue. Modern functional neurosurgery (capsulotomy, cingulotomy, deep brain stimulation) targets specific circuits with imaging guidance and is reversible (in DBS).
items.why: Therapeutic enthusiasm without rigorous evidence can produce widespread harm. Modern evidence-based standards exist because of cases like this.

items.title: Deinstitutionalisation reduced asylum populations dramatically
items.claim: Following Italy's Basaglia Law (1978), the UK's Care in the Community policy (1980s-90s) and similar reforms elsewhere, what happened to inpatient psychiatric populations?

options.text: Inpatient populations fell by 60-90% in most Western countries by 2000. Outcomes were mixed: better integration for many, but inadequate community resources left some patients homeless or in the criminal justice system
Inpatient care was completely eliminated everywhere

items.reveal:
UK psychiatric inpatient beds: ~150,000 in 1955, ~22,000 by 2010. The shift was driven by both ideology (asylum critique, e.g. Goffman 'Asylums' 1961) and pharmacology (chlorpromazine, 1952).

Where community resources followed (Trieste, Italy under Basaglia), outcomes were generally positive. Where they didn't (UK and US in different ways), gaps in care emerged — over-representation of severely mentally ill people in prisons and homelessness is widely documented.
items.why: Major mental health policy changes have decades-long consequences. The reduction in coercive asylum care was widely accepted; the under-investment in community alternatives is the unresolved part.

items.title: Ioannidis argued most published research findings are false
items.claim: John Ioannidis's 2005 PLoS Medicine paper made what claim?

options.text: Most published research findings are false — because of low prior probability of true effects, low power, flexibility in analysis, and selective reporting; the title was 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'

items.reveal:
Ioannidis used a Bayesian framework: a positive finding's probability of being true depends on prior probability of the hypothesis, power, type I error rate and bias. For exploratory research with many tested hypotheses and small studies, the probability that a 'significant' result is true can be below 50%.

The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 Science paper directly tested this in psychology: of 100 replications, 36% were significant in the same direction as the original. Effect sizes averaged about half the original. Hardly any of those original findings were obviously wrong; many were inflated by methodological flexibility.
items.why: The replication crisis isn't unique to psychology — it has hit medicine, economics, marketing and machine learning. The methodological response (preregistration, larger samples, registered reports) is reshaping research practice.

items.title: P-hacking inflates apparent significance
items.claim: Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn's 2011 'False-Positive Psychology' demonstrated that researchers can produce a 'significant' result for almost any hypothesis. How?

options.text: Through flexibility in data analysis: collecting more data after seeing p > 0.05, dropping outliers post-hoc, choosing between dependent variables, running multiple subgroups — even without intent to deceive
By using the wrong statistical software
By having too large a sample

items.reveal:
Simmons et al. showed that using a few common research practices (optional stopping, choice between similar DVs, controlling for covariates), false positive rates could rise from 5% to over 60%.

Gelman and Loken (2014) called this the 'garden of forking paths' — even without explicit p-hacking, the path through analysis can be contingent on data in ways that inflate apparent significance. Preregistration commits researchers to choices before seeing data.
items.why: P-hacking can produce false positives without anyone meaning to do anything wrong. The fix is structural: preregister, separate exploratory from confirmatory analysis, use larger samples.

items.title: Pre-registration commits to analyses before data collection
items.claim: Pre-registration of study designs and analysis plans was adopted by many psychology journals through the 2010s. What problem does it address?

options.text: It distinguishes confirmatory analyses (specified in advance) from exploratory ones (data-driven), preventing post-hoc rationalisation of decisions and reducing the garden of forking paths
It allows researchers to publish without data
It is required by law everywhere

items.reveal:
Registered Reports (introduced at Cortex in 2013, now at 300+ journals) take pre-registration further: methods are peer-reviewed and accepted before data collection, so positive and negative results have equal chance of publication.

Evidence on impact: registered reports show much higher rates of null results being published (Scheel, Schijen & Lakens 2021) and lower effect-size inflation. The OSF (Open Science Framework, 2013) provides infrastructure.
items.why: Pre-registration is a structural fix to publication bias and p-hacking. It separates testing hypotheses from generating them, which conventional analysis blurs.

items.title: Effect size matters as much as significance
items.claim: A study reports a 'highly significant' effect (p < 0.001) of a school intervention. What further information do you need?

options.text: The effect size (e.g. Cohen's d, standardised mean difference). A trivial effect can be highly significant with a large sample; a substantial effect can be non-significant with a small sample. Significance and magnitude are different questions
Only the title of the paper

items.reveal:
Cohen's d conventions (1988): 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Education research (EEF, Hattie's meta-analyses) often reports effect sizes in months of additional learning progress.

The ASA Statement on p-values (2016) explicitly warned against treating p < 0.05 as sufficient. Recommendations: report effect sizes with confidence intervals; treat 'significance' as one piece of evidence, not as a binary verdict.
items.why: Newspaper science writing usually reports significance, not magnitude. The interesting question for policy or practice is almost always how big the effect is.

items.title: Meta-analysis combines studies — but inherits their flaws
items.claim: Glass and Smith's 1977 meta-analysis pooled psychotherapy outcome studies. What's the standard caveat for any meta-analysis?

options.text: 'Garbage in, garbage out' — if individual studies are biased (publication bias, small samples, poor methods) the meta-analytic average inherits the bias. PRISMA guidelines (2009, updated 2020) standardise reporting; risk of bias assessment is essential

items.reveal:
Funnel plots can reveal publication bias (asymmetry suggests missing small studies with null results). Trim-and-fill methods attempt to correct it. PROSPERO (2011) registers planned systematic reviews.

Cochrane Reviews are widely regarded as the gold standard but even Cochrane has had to retract or revise reviews (e.g., on screening) as methods evolved.
items.why: Meta-analyses summarise evidence but don't fix bias at source. Reading meta-analyses well requires understanding what was included and what wasn't.
